speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Prime Minister regarding the report by MAS that bank customers in Singapore suffered fraudulent credit card transactions following malicious actors' diversion of SMS One-time Passwords (OTPs), whether a retrospective review will be conducted to establish whether additional customers prior to September 2020 may have been affected.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: So, with your permission, may I take all these PQs related to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS') recent announcement on the SMS one-time password (OTP) fraud, at the same time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Banks will similarly investigate any new reports by customers, including any such transactions before September 2020.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Bank customers will not have to bear any unauthorised charges in cases which are confirmed to have been enabled by SMS OTP diversion, as long as customers had taken care to protect their card information and authentication credentials.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, bank customers will not have to bear any such unauthorised charges so long as they had taken care to protect their card information and authentication credentials.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Banks have a responsibility to secure their IT systems, put in place robust measures to authenticate customer transactions and conduct active surveillance to detect unusual transactions patterns.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are required to institute robust security controls to safeguard customers’ account information and transaction data from unauthorised access and misuse.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Likewise, bank customers too have a responsibility – to protect their online banking and payment credentials for authentication such as passwords and OTPs, by inputting them only on official websites or mobile applications.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These should never be disclosed over the phone, via text message or email.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Giam had asked about the measures taken by banks and telecommunication companies to safeguard against the SMS OTP diversion attack.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While banks’ systems were secure and not the cause of these incidents, banks have further enhanced their fraud surveillance measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This includes rejecting card payments made to common merchants linked to the unauthorised transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Banks will continue to closely monitor the evolving cybersecurity landscape, and regularly review authentication mechanisms and other security measures put in place to address risks posed to customers using online financial services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As for the local telecommunication networks, IMDA, in consultation with the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), has required telco operators to put in place specialised firewalls and system safeguards to monitor and block suspicious diversions of SMS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Ms Pereira highlighted, consumers need to also take action to protect themselves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Allow me to share a few actions which consumers can focus on.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, consumers must assume that criminals will try to obtain their online banking credentials.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Criminals typically do this by tricking consumers into installing malware on their devices or disclosing their online banking username and passwords through phone calls or fake websites.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When in doubt, consumers should call the banks’ official hotlines to verify the legitimacy of requests for online banking and card credentials.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Banks work with SPF, National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC) and MoneySense, our national financial education programme, to regularly alert consumers to new methods adopted by scammers and to educate consumers on how they can protect themselves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Consumers must also develop a healthy scepticism about websites, unsolicited phone calls, messages and emails.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When making online purchases, they only should use established and reputable online services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If there is any doubt about a merchant’s legitimacy, do not proceed with the transaction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And be wary of any deal or offer that sounds too good to be true.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, consumers should set transaction notification thresholds at low levels so that unauthorised transactions are detected early.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Banks work closely with SPF and Anti-Scam Centre to exchange intelligence on emerging scam trends, so that they can take prompt action.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The sooner a report is made, the higher the likelihood that the funds can be recovered.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where bank customers suffer financial losses from fraudulent transactions, they are protected as long as they have acted responsibly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Banks are expected to consider whether the customers could have taken reasonable steps to prevent the occurrence of the fraudulent transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Bank customers will not have to incur any losses which arise from the banks’ non-compliance with MAS’ rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As criminals will continue to perpetuate new and more sophisticated methods to defraud consumers, banks, consumers and the authorities need to remain vigilant in preventing as well as detecting fraudulent transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS will continue to work with all stakeholders to ensure that e-payments remain safe and secure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A Clementi resident told me that when he disputed a credit card transaction with his bank, he was told because there was an OTP record in his phone number's name, the transaction must be genuine and therefore, cannot be challenged.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He appealed a number of times; the case was resolved.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But how many more consumers would have given up before attaining a resolution?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: First, prior to September 2020, how many reports were there of fraudulent card transactions in recent years where the victim said they did not perform the transaction nor receive the SMS OTP?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has the trend been going up, prior to the latest findings?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Second, will MAS consider looking into these earlier cases too?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Cases, which based on earlier assumptions, might have been deemed clear-cut open and shut, but given the latest revelations, might warrant repeat scrutiny?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And thirdly, can MAS reassure the public, including our Clementi residents, that agencies will continue keeping an open mind when a customer is concerned about cyber fraud affecting their credit card, involving the SMS OTP?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ultimately, everyone needs to play their part: financial institutions will have to do so, customers will have to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we clarify what the responsibilities and guidelines are, then, hopefully, we can continue collectively to do more to guard against such fraudulent transactions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given that SMS OTP diversion is something that takes place overseas where MAS has no jurisdiction, how are the banks going to prevent this from happening to their customers again?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, are banks or IMDA going to work with these overseas telcos to close these loopholes?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If so, how will they ensure that the less tech-savvy customers will not be left out?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, can MAS also require banks to allow existing customers to disable SMS multi-factor authentication for their own accounts and then use app-based authentication instead, because they are more secured?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, as I mentioned in my reply, IMDA is putting in place some safeguards with regard to how the telcos operate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this instance where it comes to SMS OTP diversion, the perpetrators needed to do several things.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One, they would have obtained the victim's personal and financial information and mobile phone number already.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That would have been compromised already, through malware, through phishing, whatever methods they would have gotten that information.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, the perpetrators would have gained access to a few overseas telco networks to compromise their system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, they would fraudulently modify the location details of the targeted victims as though these victims were overseas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, you make a transaction and the bank sends an SMS OTP through this overseas network.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This would include, for example, knowing where an individual's location is, and if you suddenly see the change in location, a red flag may be triggered, and then, the telco would then have safeguards in place to prevent the SMS from being diverted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These system safeguards are being worked on by telcos.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second question, can you please repeat the second question?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Asking the banks to use other forms of authentication besides SMS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Other forms of authentication and whether you can allow customers to opt out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As for allowing options for customers, it is something that MAS can engage the banks on, to see if the banks will be prepared to give more options for customers who feel they would prefer something more secure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I must say whatever you put in place, the perpetrators will always be looking out for new ways to identify vulnerabilities and weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this has to be a continuous effort to make sure that our systems remain secure and it requires continued vigilance by regulator, financial institutions and customers, importantly.
